body.text: In short:
The criminal trial of Alan Jones has heard Complainant H felt "disgusting and powerless" after the broadcaster allegedly touched his bottom at an event.
Mr Jones has been charged with one count of sexual touching in relation to the incident, which he has pleaded not guilty to.
What's next?
Complainant H will continue to give evidence as the trial proceeds.

A man has told the criminal trial of broadcaster Alan Jones that he felt "disgusting and powerless" and "understood what women had been going through" after Mr Jones allegedly touched his bottom at an event.
The fourth of five male complainants in the trial, Complainant H, has begun to give evidence against Mr Jones, who is facing 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching in the NSW Local Court.
Mr Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
The man, who was an executive and decades younger than Mr Jones, has told the court he met the broadcaster for the first time at an event more than five years ago.
He said Mr Jones was standing next to him at the event, when the former radio host "placed his hand on the top of my back and went slowly down my back and then rested it on my bottom".
Complainant H said he did not say anything to Mr Jones at the time, and does not recall reacting physically because he "didn't want to cause a scene".
"I thought that could potentially ruin the night,"he said.
'Disgusting and powerless'
The man said he told his boss what allegedly happened as he was leaving the event, and said the woman was "angry" and made him feel supported.
Complainant H said he told a second colleague what happened a couple of days later.
"I said that I felt disgusting and powerless and that's really the first time I've understood what women have been going through for all these years," he said.
Mr Jones has been charged with one count of sexual touching in relation to the event.
The executive gave evidence that in 2023, he saw an article in the Sydney Morning Herald which contained allegations about Mr Jones.
He said he contacted the author, journalist Kate McClymont, and told her what allegedly happened to him at the event.
The executive said he did not give the journalist permission to tell his story, but in May 2024 he noticed a second story published by Ms McClymont with his allegations included, but not his name.
Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright SC whether he authorised that information to be published, the man said he did not.
"Were you upset about that?" Ms Wright asked.
'I hope [Jones] gets what he deserves'

Under cross examination, Complainant H was questioned about his memory of the event, and accepted he gave different people, including police, different accounts of when during the event that the alleged touch happened.
The complainant told the court he could not recall exactly at what point of the event the incident occurred.
He also accepted he did not make a formal complaint when he told his boss, nor did he write down notes of the alleged assault.
The court heard the man spoke to police in June 2024, after Ms McClymont asked him if she could pass on his details to an officer.

In a text exchange with Ms McClymont, Complainant H gave the journalist permission for police to get in contact, and said, "good, I hope [Alan Jones] gets what he deserves. I'm happy to talk to the police."
Complainant asked about 'police strategy'
Late on Tuesday, the executive accepted he had discussed what the "police strategy" may be in text messages to a colleague, who he allegedly confided in about the incident.
During the text exchange, Complainant H allegedly said "everything needs to be perfect when they [police] charge him", while referencing how long the police investigation may take.
The court heard when the complainant was asked during a meeting with the prosecution what he meant by that message he told them: "Like all the stories, everyone's all need to align basically."
Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC asked the man if police had spoken to him about "tendency evidence" during their investigation, to which he asked, "what is tendency evidence?".
The court heard the complainant sent another text message to his colleague saying he hoped he could "help get Alan for others".
"I just didn't realise what had happened to me was a crime, I thought it was being used as a pattern of behaviour,"the man said.
Complainant H agreed with Ms Bashir that he spoke positively about Mr Jones in an email exchange with the veteran broadcaster shortly following the event.
Ms Bashir raised other emails just days after the alleged sexual touching that showed Complainant H had also advocated to mutual contacts for Mr Jones to be invited to similar events in the future.
The court heard the man told police in an interview that he had "never been a fan [of Mr Jones], just have had very different political views".
"I don't know too much about his politics I just know he [Mr Jones] is conservative," he told the court.
Complainant H accepted he had previously sent messages referencing Mr Jones and former Wallaby Israel Folau.
The man said he knew Mr Jones had been a "staunch defender" of Mr Folau after the rugby player made a post to social media, which included the phrase "hell awaits homosexuals".
Complainant H appeared calm as he repeatedly denied Ms Bashir's suggestions that Mr Jones had not sexually touched him.

"Mr Jones did not run his hand down your back [at the event]?" Ms Bashir suggested. "Yes, he did," Complainant H replied. "He did not rest his hand on the top of your buttocks?" Ms Bashir suggested. "Yes, he did," Complainant H replied. "He did not touch you inappropriately in any fashion?" Ms Bashir suggested. "He absolutely did," Complainant H replied.
"Mr Jones did not run his hand down your back [at the event]?" Ms Bashir suggested.
"Yes, he did," Complainant H replied.
"He did not rest his hand on the top of your buttocks?" Ms Bashir suggested.
"Yes, he did," Complainant H replied.
"He did not touch you inappropriately in any fashion?" Ms Bashir suggested.
"He absolutely did," Complainant H replied.
The trial continues.
